before.content_html:
The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells divide to produce new cells for growth, repair and replacement. The process of cell division in body cells is called mitosis. Mitosis is part of the cell cycle — the repeating sequence of growth and division that cells go through.

The cell cycle has several stages. Before mitosis begins, the cell goes through interphase, during which the cell grows, carries out its normal functions, and makes a copy of every chromosome (DNA replication). Once interphase is complete, mitosis can begin.

The Edexcel specification requires you to know the stages of mitosis:

  • Prophase — chromosomes condense and become visible. The nuclear membrane starts to break down.
  • Metaphase — chromosomes line up along the middle (equator) of the cell.
  • Anaphase — the two copies of each chromosome are pulled apart to opposite ends (poles) of the cell by spindle fibres.
  • Telophase — a new nuclear membrane forms around each set of chromosomes. The chromosomes begin to uncoil.
  • Cytokinesis — the cytoplasm divides, producing two separate daughter cells.

Key Fact

Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to each other AND to the parent cell. Each daughter cell is diploid — it has the full set of chromosomes. Remember the order: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase (PMAT).

Importance of Mitosis

Mitosis is important for three key reasons:

  • Growth — organisms grow by producing more cells through mitosis.
  • Repair — damaged or worn-out cells are replaced by identical new cells made through mitosis (e.g. skin cells replacing a wound).
  • Asexual reproduction — some organisms reproduce by mitosis alone, producing offspring that are genetically identical to the parent (clones). For example, strawberry plants send out runners, and bacteria divide by binary fission.

Cancer

Cancer occurs when changes (mutations) in a cell's DNA cause the cell to divide uncontrollably. Normal cells have checkpoints in the cell cycle that prevent division when it is not needed. In cancer, these controls fail. The rapidly dividing cells form a mass called a tumour. Some tumours are benign (stay in one place), but malignant tumours can spread to other parts of the body.

Growth in Organisms

Growth happens differently in animals and plants:

  • Animals grow by cell division (mitosis) and then cell differentiation — cells become specialised for particular functions.
  • Plants grow by cell division, cell elongation (cells stretch and lengthen), and cell differentiation.

Percentile charts are used to monitor growth in children. They show how a child's height or weight compares to others of the same age. For example, if a child is on the 75th percentile for height, it means 75% of children of the same age are shorter. Doctors use percentile charts to check for potential growth problems — a child who drops significantly across percentile lines might need further investigation.

Key Fact

Plant growth differs from animal growth because it involves cell elongation as well as cell division and differentiation. Most plant growth occurs at the tips of roots and shoots, where meristems are located.

Stem Cells

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells — they have not yet become specialised. They can divide to produce more stem cells or differentiate into different types of specialised cell.

There are different types of stem cell:

  • Embryonic stem cells — found in early embryos. These can differentiate into almost any type of cell in the body. They have the greatest potential for medical use.
  • Adult stem cells — found in some adult tissues (e.g. bone marrow). These can only differentiate into a limited range of cell types. For example, bone marrow stem cells can produce different types of blood cell.
  • Meristems — found in plants at the tips of roots and shoots. Meristem cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant's life. This is why plants continue growing for their entire lifespan.
Stem Cells in Medicine: Benefits and Risks

Stem cells offer exciting possibilities in medicine. They could be used to replace damaged or diseased cells — for example, replacing faulty insulin-producing cells in type 1 diabetes, or repairing damaged nerve cells after spinal injuries.

However, there are also risks and ethical concerns. The use of embryonic stem cells is controversial because it involves the destruction of embryos. There are also medical risks — stem cells could divide uncontrollably and cause tumours. The body's immune system may reject transplanted stem cells. Adult stem cell treatments are less controversial but are more limited in what they can differentiate into.

Key Fact

In the exam, you may be asked to discuss the benefits and risks of stem cell use. Benefits: potential to treat diseases like diabetes, Parkinson's, and paralysis. Risks: tumour formation, immune rejection, ethical issues around embryo destruction. Balance both sides in your answer.

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between how animals and plants grow.
practice_questions.marks: Plants grow by cell elongation as well as cell division, whereas animals grow by cell division only (1). Plant growth continues throughout the organism's life (at meristems), whereas most animal growth stops at adulthood (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why embryonic stem cells are considered more useful than adult stem cells for medical treatment.
practice_questions.marks: Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any type of cell (1). Adult stem cells can only differentiate into a limited range of cell types (1). So embryonic stem cells have greater potential to treat a wider range of diseases (1).

before.content_html:
Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is the process by which humans choose organisms with desirable characteristics and breed them together. This is repeated over many generations until the desired trait is strongly expressed in the population.

Selective breeding has been used for thousands of years. Examples include breeding food plants for higher yield, disease resistance or improved taste, and breeding domesticated animals for traits such as increased milk production in cows, faster growth in chickens or tameness in dogs.

The process works because the parents with the best characteristics are selected, so their alleles are more likely to be passed on. Over many generations, the frequency of the desirable alleles increases in the population.

Key Fact

Selective breeding: choose parents with desirable traits → breed them → select the best offspring → repeat over many generations. Used to improve food plants and domesticated animals.

A major risk of selective breeding is inbreeding. Because only organisms with similar desirable traits are bred, the gene pool narrows. This reduces genetic variation, making the population more vulnerable to new diseases or environmental changes. In animals, inbreeding can also lead to health problems — for example, breathing difficulties in flat-faced dog breeds.

What Is Genetic Engineering?

Genetic engineering is the process of modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics. Unlike selective breeding, which works within a species, genetic engineering can transfer genes between completely different species. An organism that contains a gene from a different species is called a genetically modified organism (GMO) or transgenic organism.

The Main Stages of Genetic Engineering

The Edexcel specification requires you to describe the main stages of genetic engineering, including the use of restriction enzymes, ligase, sticky ends and vectors.

Step 1 — Identify and cut out the desired gene. Restriction enzymes are used to cut the desired gene out of the DNA of the donor organism. These enzymes cut at specific base sequences, leaving short unpaired stretches of bases called sticky ends.

Step 2 — Open the vector. The same restriction enzyme is used to cut open a vector — a carrier molecule that will transport the gene into the host organism. Common vectors include bacterial plasmids and viruses. Because the same restriction enzyme is used, the vector has complementary sticky ends.

Step 3 — Insert the gene. The desired gene is inserted into the vector. The complementary sticky ends of the gene and the vector pair up. Ligase enzyme is then used to seal the gene into the vector by joining the sugar-phosphate backbone, creating recombinant DNA.

Step 4 — Transfer to host organism. The vector carries the gene into the host organism’s cells. If the gene is successfully taken up, the host organism will produce the protein coded for by the inserted gene, giving it the desired characteristic.

Key Fact

Genetic engineering: restriction enzymes cut out the gene (leaving sticky ends) → same enzyme opens the vector → gene inserted, sticky ends pair up → ligase seals the join → vector transfers gene to host organism.

Examples of Genetic Engineering

In agriculture, crops such as soya and maize have been genetically modified to be resistant to herbicides or to produce their own insecticide (Bt crops). Golden rice has been engineered to produce beta-carotene (vitamin A) to help prevent deficiency in developing countries.

In medicine, the gene for human insulin has been inserted into bacteria. These bacteria are grown in fermenters and produce large quantities of human insulin to treat diabetes. This replaced insulin extracted from pig or cow pancreases, which sometimes caused allergic reactions.

Benefits and Risks of Genetic Engineering and Selective Breeding

The Edexcel specification requires you to evaluate the benefits and risks of both genetic engineering and selective breeding in modern agriculture and medicine, including practical and ethical implications.

Benefits of genetic engineering: genes can be transferred between species that could never breed naturally; crops can be made pest-resistant, reducing pesticide use; medicines like insulin can be produced cheaply and reliably; Golden Rice could reduce vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

Risks and concerns: GM crops could cross-pollinate with wild plants, spreading modified genes into the environment in unpredictable ways; there are concerns about the long-term effects of eating GM food (though no evidence of harm has been found); some people have ethical objections to ‘playing God’ with organisms’ DNA; GM seeds are often patented, making farmers dependent on seed companies.

Selective breeding is considered more ‘natural’ but reduces genetic diversity, which can cause health problems and makes populations vulnerable to disease. Genetic engineering is faster and more precise, but raises more ethical and environmental concerns.
